title: Targeted search: finding the clients that fit your service for Car detailing
audience: Solo operators and team owners in any service business who want more work from clients that suit their service, their area and their job size.
learningOutcomes: Build a prospect list that is scored against written fit criteria for service area, job size and repeat need.
Identify public signals that a client need is starting, and explain why each one is a reasonable reason to make contact.
Write a first approach that makes one specific, verifiable observation, offers one small next step and can be declined easily.

instruction.heading: Decide what work you want before you look for it
instruction.body: Write down the packages you do well, the price band you can sustain, the suburbs you can reach without losing money on travel, and how often each kind of client needs you. A Sydney vendor list sets Basic, Mid-level and Premium ranges (Schmicko, modified 8 August 2026). Use those ranges to test whether your price band is realistic, not as a market average. Write one short profile for each segment on your list, as business.gov.au suggests when identifying a target market (business.gov.au, 24 September 2024). These criteria are the filter for everything that follows. If you cannot state them, you cannot tell a good lead from a poor one.

instruction.heading: Build a scored prospect list
instruction.body: Keep every candidate in one list with a fit column and a status column. Score each prospect as strong fit, possible fit or not a fit, using the written criteria. Ask whether it sits inside your service area, whether it has a repeat need, whether you can reach the person who decides, and whether the work falls within the licence and insurance you hold. The research did not source a prospect type for car detailing. The one channel it found is dealer work, from a consultant article that describes dealers sending business but gives no terms (carwash.com, no date shown). Fleet operators and rental companies are not sourced, so add them only on your own judgement and mark that judgement on the list. Record the date each entry was added and where its details came from. Use only business contact details published for business use. Do not use bought or harvested lists. ACMA's guidance says buying a list does not remove the need to show consent.

instruction.heading: Watch for signals that a need is starting
instruction.body: A signal is a public event that makes a need more likely soon. For car detailing the research found few sourced signals, so treat any signal as a prompt to qualify rather than proof of demand. Public tender registers show what government agencies buy. In Victoria, Buying for Victoria lists current and past tenders and lets suppliers set alerts (Buying for Victoria, 7 August 2026). AusTender does the same federally. Whether a vehicle detailing service appears on either register was not checked. Use signals to decide when to make contact, not to build a profile of individuals. Do not monitor private people, and do not approach a private car owner from a registration or other private record.

instruction.heading: Make a first approach that is specific and easy to decline
instruction.body: A useful first message does three things. It states how you came to know about the business. It makes one specific observation that you can verify from public view or from the business's own published material, such as a dealership's service list that does not mention detailing, which is an illustrative example. It then offers one small next step, such as a written quote for a defined fleet or a fifteen-minute call. Keep the message short, do not overstate what you know, and make it simple to say no. The ACCC's 2026 review of unsolicited selling found that many approaches were pressured or misleading and that many salespeople did not identify themselves (ACCC, 28 July 2026), so a specific, honest message that names you is a practical advantage. Once a prospect replies, confirm the scope, your capacity and the deadline before you quote, as Business Queensland advises (Business Queensland, 16 November 2022; Queensland guidance).

instruction.heading: Follow up on a fixed schedule and stop when asked
instruction.body: Decide in advance how many follow-ups you will send and how far apart. A common pattern is one reminder after a week and one final message after a further two weeks, followed by a pause. If a prospect says no, or asks you to stop, remove them from the list at once and record the request with its date. At the end of each month, review which fit tier and which signal produced replies that became paid work. Silence is not consent to keep contacting someone.

procedure: Write the package, area, price band and repeat-need criteria for the detailing work you want.
Build the prospect list and score each entry as strong fit, possible fit or not a fit, with a reason.
Choose two or three public signals to watch and note the date each one is seen.
Write one first message for each fit tier, with a stated source, one verifiable observation and one small next step.
Check each message against the electronic message rules and the licence and insurance rules for the work before sending.
Send to strong-fit prospects first, then follow up on the fixed schedule.
Remove anyone who asks you to stop, and review the results at the end of the month.

workedExamples.situation: A detailer covers three suburbs. A dealership in one of them has a published general enquiries email address on its website, and its public service page does not mention detailing. The owner wants to email the service manager.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Should the owner send a sales email now, and what should it contain?
workedExamples.reasoning: Publishing a business address does not by itself permit a commercial message. The Spam Act covers business addresses too, so the owner first checks whether the dealership has agreed to receive such messages or has invited contact. If neither applies, the owner does not send the sales email and waits for an invitation or uses a route the dealership has agreed to. A phone call to a registered number is limited by the Do Not Call Register rules, so the owner checks the register first. Any message that does go out names how the owner learned of the business, makes one specific observation from the public service page, offers one small next step and includes the sender's details and an opt-out. The owner does not use private details of any individual.

equipmentAndPpe: Prospect list in a spreadsheet or notebook, with fit and status columns
Written fit criteria for service area, package and repeat need
Message templates checked against the electronic message rules
No PPE is needed for desk work; any site visit follows the site's own safety rules

commonErrors.error: Sending the same message to everyone on a broad list at once.
commonErrors.prevention: Score the list first, write one message for each fit tier, and start with the strong-fit tier.

commonErrors.error: Using private information about an individual, such as a registration record, to make contact.
commonErrors.prevention: Use only contact details published for business use, or details the person has given you for this purpose.

commonErrors.error: Pitching a service that you are not licensed or insured to deliver.
commonErrors.prevention: Check the licence and insurance before outreach, and remove that service from the message.

commonErrors.error: Following up without a limit, or continuing after a request to stop. Gap: no verified prospect channel exists for car detailing.
commonErrors.prevention: Set a fixed number of follow-ups and a stop rule, and record every stop request.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Do not offer a licensed or authorised service in outreach unless you hold the licence that the state or territory where the work is done requires. This lesson does not grant any licence. Licence rules differ between states and territories, so check the rule for each one you work in.

Commercial electronic messages, including email and text, are regulated by the Spam Act 2003 (Cth). ACMA's Spam Act obligations page (last updated 28 March 2019) says the Act also covers business addresses, and that publishing an address does not by itself permit commercial messages. ACMA's avoid-spam guidance says marketing messages need consent, that consent should be recorded, and that unsubscribe requests must be honoured within five working days. The Act text was not read for this lesson.

Information on a public listing does not by itself permit contact about anything. If the Privacy Act applies to your business, OAIC's guidance on direct marketing (APP 7) says that public information is not exempt from the direct-marketing rules. Use only contact details published for business use, keep them secure, and stop using them when someone objects.

qualityStandard: Every prospect on the list has a fit score, a reason for that score and a recorded source for its contact details.
Every first message contains one verifiable observation and one small, easy-to-decline next step.
No contact is made using private information, and every stop request is recorded and actioned.
documentationEvidence: Prospect list with fit score, reason, status, source and date added.
Signal log with the date each public signal was seen.
Stop-request record with the date it was actioned.
summary: Define the detailing work you want first, then filter prospects against that definition.
Watch public signals, and never use private information to make contact.
Gap: no verified client channel exists for car detailing. Test every prospect type on your own evidence before relying on it.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which prospect should you contact first?
options: A one-off job well outside your service area, because it looks large
A fleet operator with several sites inside your service area that you already visit
Any business that has a website, because it probably spends money on services

knowledgeChecks.question: A dealership's general email address is published on its website. What is the most appropriate first step?
options: Send a sales email to the general address, since it is published
Check consent or an invitation under the Spam Act before sending any commercial message
Use a private social media account of a salesperson to send the same message

knowledgeChecks.question: Before you send a commercial email to a prospect, what should you do?
options: Check that the subject line is fun and the message is short
Ask the prospect to like your social media page first
Confirm the Spam Act 2003 requirements in current ACMA guidance

officialReferences.title: Avoid sending spam (ACMA)
officialReferences.covers: Says a business needs consent before sending marketing messages, and consent must be recorded; each message must identify the sender and include correct contact details; every commercial message must include an unsubscribe option that works for at least 30 days and is honoured within 5 working days. Does not name the Spam Act 2003 or cover privacy law. Publisher: ACMA.

officialReferences.title: Chapter 7: APP 7 direct marketing (OAIC)
officialReferences.pageDate: page modified 16 October 2023; version 1.1 dated 22 July 2019
officialReferences.covers: Says the direct-marketing rules apply to personal information that is publicly available, with no general exemption for public information. Applies only where the Privacy Act covers the business. Publisher: OAIC.
